NWSI 10-513 WFO Winter Weather Products Specification (Nov 6, 2024)

fundamentals.tagline: Four words carry the whole system. Learn what each demands of you.
fundamentals.intro: Four tiers carry almost every hazard NWS issues. Knowing which tier you are looking at tells you what is expected of you before you read a single detail.
essentials: Watch means be prepared. Warning means take action. Advisory means be aware.
Your local NWS office issues the warnings. The Storm Prediction Center issues the convective watches.
Not every warning sends an alert to phones.
Convective criteria are national. Most other thresholds are set by your local office.

sections.heading: The four tiers

tiers.name: Watch
tiers.means: Conditions are favorable. The event is not certain.

tiers.name: Warning
tiers.means: The hazard is imminent or occurring.

tiers.name: Advisory
tiers.means: Hazardous or inconvenient, but below warning criteria.

tiers.name: Statement
tiers.means: Updates an active warning, or covers sub-severe conditions.

sections.note: An advisory is not an all-clear, and it does not promise an upgrade. Advisories exist across the winter, wind, dust, fog, heat, flood and marine programs.

sections.heading: Who issues what
points: Tornado Warnings and Severe Thunderstorm Warnings come from your local Weather Forecast Office (WFO).
The Storm Prediction Center issues convective watches and outlooks, never the warnings.
After SPC issues a watch, your WFO issues Watch County Notifications naming the counties included.

sections.heading: Reading a VTEC string
sections.intro: Every watch, warning and advisory carries one of these machine strings. Two parts matter most to you: the phenomenon and the significance.

sections.heading: Polygons and phone alerts
points: Storm-based polygon warnings are drawn to the projected threat area rather than following county lines, which cuts down on over-warning people outside the storm path.
Wireless Emergency Alerts are selective by design, so the alert keeps its meaning. Not every warning fires one.
Some products only push a WEA when a specific damage threat tag is present.
WEA targets phones geographically, not by subscription. NOAA Weather Radio is a separate path.

fundamentals.local: Convective criteria (58 mph, 1.00 inch hail) are national. Most non-convective thresholds, including winter storm snow amounts, heat index triggers, wind advisory speeds and red flag humidity, are set by your local office and differ across the country. Treating another office's number as national is the single most common source of bad spotter training.

changes.what: NWS plans to retire the terms Advisory and Special Weather Statement in favor of plain-language headlines. Watch and Warning are staying.
changes.when: Announced, repeatedly delayed. NWS says no earlier than calendar 2026 and has promised at least six months notice. Advisories are still live products.

quickChecks.q: Conditions are favorable but the event is not certain. Which tier is that, and what do you do?
quickChecks.a: A Watch. Be prepared. Warning means take action, Advisory means be aware.

quickChecks.q: Who issues the Tornado Warning for your county, and who issued the watch before it?
quickChecks.a: Your local forecast office issues the warning. The Storm Prediction Center issued the watch.

quickChecks.q: Your phone stayed silent. Does that mean there is no warning near you?
quickChecks.a: No. WEA is selective by design, and not every warning sends a phone alert. Keep a second path, like the app or NOAA Weather Radio.

quickChecks.q: In /O.NEW.KMAF.SV.W.0043/, what are SV and W?
quickChecks.a: SV is the phenomenon, severe thunderstorm. W is the significance, Warning.

convective-warnings.tagline: Two numbers, three tags, and which storms buzz phones.
convective-warnings.intro: This is the module where a wrong answer has real operational consequences, which is why it needs 85 percent to pass. The criteria here are national, so these numbers are the same wherever you spot.
essentials: Severe Thunderstorm Warning: 58 mph winds or 1.00 inch hail. Either one alone is enough.
A quarter is 1.00 inch. That is the size that matters.
Only a Destructive tag sends a severe thunderstorm warning to phones.
Every tornado warning goes to phones, whatever the tag.

sections.heading: The two numbers
sections.body: Wind gusts of 58 mph and/or hail of 1.00 inch. Either one alone is enough. The hail criterion rose from 0.75 inch to 1.00 inch in 2010.
points: 58 mph is the conversion of 50 knots (57.5 mph, rounded). Warning text often renders it as 60 mph.
Sub-severe storms, roughly 40 to 57 mph gusts or hail under 1 inch, get a Special Weather Statement rather than a warning.

sections.heading: Hail size, to scale
sections.note: Report hail by comparing to a coin or ball, never a guess in inches. A quarter is the coin that matters.

sections.heading: Severe Thunderstorm Warning damage threat tags

tags.name: Considerable
tags.criteria: At least 70 mph and/or 1.75 inch hail

tags.name: Destructive
tags.criteria: At least 80 mph and/or 2.75 inch hail

sections.note: The highest qualifying value of either wind or hail sets the tag. If your phone buzzes for a severe thunderstorm warning, it is the top tier.

sections.heading: Tornado Warning tags

tags.name: Base
tags.criteria: Radar-indicated or reliably reported tornado, no tag line

tags.name: Considerable
tags.criteria: Elevated threat. This is the tag that carries PARTICULARLY DANGEROUS SITUATION wording in the warning

points: Every tornado warning fires a WEA regardless of tag. This is the opposite of severe thunderstorm warnings.
Catastrophic is exceedingly rare: reliable sources or clear radar evidence confirm a damaging tornado, and a severe threat to life with catastrophic damage is occurring.
A Tornado Warning may be issued on radar indication OR a reliable spotter report. Both demand the same protective action.

myths.myth: Severe Thunderstorm Warnings go Base, Considerable, Catastrophic.
myths.truth: They top out at Destructive. Tornado and Flash Flood Warnings are the ones that top out at Catastrophic.

quickChecks.q: What are the two numbers that make a storm severe?
quickChecks.a: 58 mph wind gusts and 1.00 inch hail, quarter size. Either one alone is enough.

quickChecks.q: Your phone buzzes with a Severe Thunderstorm Warning. What does that tell you about the tag?
quickChecks.a: It is the top tier, Destructive: at least 80 mph and/or baseball size hail. Base and Considerable do not alert phones.

quickChecks.q: Which warnings top out at Catastrophic, and which at Destructive?
quickChecks.a: Tornado and Flash Flood Warnings top out at Catastrophic. Severe Thunderstorm Warnings top out at Destructive.

quickChecks.q: A storm has 45 mph gusts and pea size hail. What product covers it?
quickChecks.a: A Special Weather Statement. It is below the severe thresholds.

quickChecks.q: Does a radar-indicated Tornado Warning demand less action than a confirmed one?
quickChecks.a: No. Both demand the same protective action.

watches-outlooks.tagline: The products that let you position instead of react.
watches-outlooks.intro: The products that arrive before the warning. These are what let you position and prepare rather than react.
essentials: SPC issues the watches. Your local office issues the warnings.
Risk levels run Marginal, Slight, Enhanced, Moderate, High. Marginal is first, not Slight.
Tornadoes still happen inside a Severe Thunderstorm Watch.
Do not wait for a watch to start operations.

sections.heading: SPC Convective Outlook risk levels
sections.note: Marginal comes before Slight. This ordering is a frequent trip-up.

sections.heading: PDS wording
points: PDS stands for Particularly Dangerous Situation, used in rare cases.
A PDS Tornado Watch signals potential for long-lived, strong to violent tornadoes.
PDS wording can also accompany severe thunderstorm watches for intense convective windstorms such as high-end derechos.

sections.heading: Mesoscale Discussions
sections.body: An SPC Mesoscale Discussion describes short-term evolving conditions and often precedes a watch, frequently stating watch probability and timing. SPC aims to issue one an hour or two before the watch itself.

myths.myth: It is only a Severe Thunderstorm Watch, so no tornadoes today.
myths.truth: Brief tornadoes occur inside severe thunderstorm watches regularly, especially with QLCS or squall-line circulations that give little lead time.

myths.myth: Wait for the watch before starting operations.
myths.truth: Outlooks, the Hazardous Weather Outlook and Mesoscale Discussions all come first, and warnings are sometimes issued with no watch in effect at all.

quickChecks.q: Put these in order, lowest first: Slight, Marginal, Enhanced.
quickChecks.a: Marginal, then Slight, then Enhanced. Marginal is level 1 of 5.

quickChecks.q: A Severe Thunderstorm Watch is up. Can a tornado still happen?
quickChecks.a: Yes. Brief tornadoes occur inside severe thunderstorm watches, especially in QLCS squall lines, with little lead time.

quickChecks.q: What often shows up an hour or two before a watch?
quickChecks.a: An SPC Mesoscale Discussion, frequently stating watch probability and timing.

quickChecks.q: Should you wait for the watch before starting operations?
quickChecks.a: No. Outlooks, the HWO and Mesoscale Discussions come first, and warnings sometimes arrive with no watch at all.

flooding.tagline: Rewritten in 2021. Most older training is wrong here.
flooding.intro: The flood program was significantly restructured in November 2021. Most older spotter training is wrong here, so pay attention to what no longer exists.
essentials: Flash flooding is rapid. A Flood Warning is slower or longer lasting.
Base flash flood warnings do not go to phones. Considerable and Catastrophic do.
Since 2021 the Flash Flood Watch only covers dam and levee failure, ice jams and burn scars.
Flash flooding happens in places where it is not raining.

sections.heading: Flash Flood Warning
sections.body: Issued when life- or property-threatening short-term flooding is imminent or occurring, whether from heavy rainfall or from a dam or levee failure.

sections.heading: Flash Flood Warning damage threat tags
sections.note: Base-tagged flash flood warnings deliberately do not fire a WEA, an impact-based change rolled out in 2019 and 2020. Before that every flash flood warning buzzed, which diluted the alert.

rows.old: Flash Flood Watch for rain-driven events
rows.note: The Flash Flood Watch survives only for dam or levee failure, ice jams, and excessive rain over burn scars or debris-flow-prone terrain.

rows.old: Five advisories: Urban and Small Stream, Arroyo and Small Stream, Small Stream, Flood, Hydrologic
rows.note: If training material still lists Urban and Small Stream Flood Advisory as a distinct product, it is out of date.

sections.heading: Flash Flood Warning versus Flood Warning

a.title: Flash Flood Warning
rows: Intense rain, dam or levee failure

b.title: Flood Warning
rows: Longer, persists after the flash threat ends

sections.note: The difference is onset speed and rate of rise, not severity.

sections.heading: Flood Advisory
sections.body: Ponding on roads, minor stream overflow: flooding that causes inconvenience rather than immediate danger. It is not an all-clear. If caution is ignored it can still threaten life or property, and conditions can escalate to a warning.

sections.heading: Dry ground is not safe ground

myths.myth: It is not raining here, so flash flooding cannot reach me.
myths.truth: Runoff from upstream, burn scars, and dam or levee failure all produce flash flooding under clear skies. Critical in arroyo and desert terrain.

points: Flood Watches give hours of preparation lead time. Flash Flood Warnings are short-fused.

quickChecks.q: Which flash flood tags alert phones?
quickChecks.a: Considerable and Catastrophic. Base does not.

quickChecks.q: What tag does a Flash Flood Emergency carry?
quickChecks.a: Catastrophic.

quickChecks.q: It is dry where you stand. Can flash flooding still reach you?
quickChecks.a: Yes. Upstream rain, burn scars, and dam or levee failure produce flash floods under clear skies.

quickChecks.q: Since 2021, when does a Flash Flood Watch still get issued?
quickChecks.a: Only for dam or levee failure, ice jams, and burn scar or debris flow terrain. Ordinary rain threats use the Flood Watch.

winter.tagline: Rebuilt in October 2024. Several products no longer exist.
winter.intro: The cold-weather headlines were rebuilt on October 1, 2024. Several products you may have trained on no longer exist under those names.
essentials: Wind Chill products are gone. They are Extreme Cold Warning and Cold Weather Advisory now.
Blizzard is about wind and visibility for 3 hours, not snow totals.
A ground blizzard needs no falling snow at all.
Snow amounts for a Winter Storm Warning are set by your local office.

sections.heading: The October 2024 rebuild

rows.note: New VTEC code CW.Y. The old WC phenomenon code was retired outright.
Hard freeze wording now rides in the product body when it applies.

sections.note: The renames reflect that dangerous cold does not require wind. The cold products are now issued on temperature or wind chill, either one.

sections.heading: Blizzard Warning: three things at once

items.title: Under 1/4 mile
items.detail: Visibility in considerable falling and/or blowing snow

sections.banner: All three together. No snowfall total required.
points: Blizzard criteria are about wind and visibility duration, not snowfall totals. No specific accumulation is required.
Snow does not have to be falling. Blowing and drifting of existing snow can produce blizzard conditions under a clear sky, known as a ground blizzard.

sections.heading: Snow Squall Warning
sections.body: A short-lived, intense burst of snow with strong winds causing sudden whiteout and flash freezing. Polygon-based and short-fused. Accumulation is usually minor. The hazard is sudden visibility loss and icing, which drives multi-vehicle pileups.
points: Fires a WEA only when it carries the significant tag, so the alert is reserved for substantial threats to safe travel.
Not issued where a Winter Storm Warning or Blizzard Warning is already active for the same area.
It can be issued during a Winter Weather Advisory when conditions briefly turn much worse.

sections.heading: The rest of the winter suite

rows: Roughly 1/4 inch or more of ice accretion, enough to bring down limbs and power lines
A significant winter event that may combine snow, sleet, ice or blowing snow
Wintry precipitation below warning criteria but enough to cause travel difficulty

sections.note: The Lake Effect Snow Warning was folded into the Winter Storm Warning for the 2017-18 season, then reinstated effective October 2019 after partner pushback. Offices may use either product.

winter.local: Winter Storm Warning accumulation thresholds, Winter Weather Advisory thresholds, and exact Ice Storm Warning accretion amounts are all set locally and vary widely by region. Blizzard criteria are the reliable national numbers in this module.

quickChecks.q: How much snow does a Blizzard Warning require?
quickChecks.a: None. It is wind of 35+ mph, visibility under 1/4 mile, for 3 or more hours. The snow can be entirely blowing snow, a ground blizzard.

quickChecks.q: What replaced the Wind Chill Advisory?
quickChecks.a: The Cold Weather Advisory, in October 2024. Wind Chill products are gone, and dangerous cold no longer requires wind.

quickChecks.q: When does a Snow Squall Warning alert phones?
quickChecks.a: Only when it carries the significant tag.

quickChecks.q: Is a Snow Squall Warning issued inside an active Winter Storm Warning?
quickChecks.a: No, they are kept separate. It can be issued during a Winter Weather Advisory if conditions briefly turn much worse.

non-precip.tagline: Mostly local numbers, one big rename, and the wind-source rule.
non-precip.intro: The Non-Precipitation Weather program. This is the most heavily local module in the bank, so treat most numbers here as typical rather than universal.
essentials: Excessive Heat became Extreme Heat in 2025. The Heat Advisory did not change.
58 mph from a storm is a Severe Thunderstorm Warning. The same wind with no storm is a High Wind Warning.
Dust Storm Warning means visibility of 1/4 mile or less.
Most thresholds in this module are local, not national.

sections.heading: The March 2025 heat rename
sections.note: Only the watch and warning were renamed, aligning the language with the Extreme Cold products. The Heat Advisory kept its name.

sections.heading: Dust products
points: Dust Storm Warning: visibility reduced to 1/4 mile or less, usually with winds of 25 mph or greater. The classic case is a convectively driven outflow dust wall.
Blowing Dust Warning: the same 1/4 mile visibility, from widespread wind-driven dust rather than a storm outflow.
Dust Advisory: short-duration dangerous blowing dust, visibility between 1 mile and 1/4 mile.
Blowing Dust Advisory: widespread dust in that same visibility band over an extended period.
Both advisories mean stay alert and consider delaying travel. Visibility of 1/4 mile or less is what makes it a warning.

sections.heading: Fog, wind, and cold

rows: Widespread visibility below 1/4 mile for an extended period
Non-convective sustained winds around 40 mph for an hour or more, or gusts to 58 mph for any duration
At or below 32 degrees during the growing season, generally sustained
Near but above freezing, with light winds and clear skies favoring frost

sections.note: Outside the growing season a Freeze Warning is usually not issued.

myths.myth: 58 mph always means a Severe Thunderstorm Warning.
myths.truth: Only when a thunderstorm produces it. The same 58 mph from gradient wind is a High Wind Warning. The source decides the product: convective winds fall under the severe program, synoptic winds under the non-precipitation program.

non-precip.local: Heat criteria vary substantially by office and climate zone. What triggers a warning in the desert Southwest differs from the upper Midwest. High Wind Warning thresholds are likewise locally set. Dense Fog Advisory visibility varies by office.

quickChecks.q: 58 mph winds and not a storm in sight. What product?
quickChecks.a: High Wind Warning. The same speed from a thunderstorm is a Severe Thunderstorm Warning. The source decides.

quickChecks.q: What visibility makes dust a warning rather than an advisory?
quickChecks.a: 1/4 mile or less. The advisories cover 1 mile down to 1/4 mile.

quickChecks.q: What was renamed in March 2025, and what kept its name?
quickChecks.a: Excessive Heat Watch and Warning became Extreme Heat Watch and Warning. The Heat Advisory kept its name.

quickChecks.q: Are heat thresholds the same everywhere?
quickChecks.a: No. Heat criteria are set locally and vary by office and climate zone.

fire-weather.tagline: Structure over numbers. The numbers are local.
fire-weather.intro: Red Flag Warnings depend on fuels as well as weather, and the numeric criteria are entirely local. What matters here is the structure, not the numbers.
essentials: Red Flag needs dangerous weather and dry fuels together, not just wind.
Fire Weather Watch is 18 to 96 hours out. Red Flag Warning is high confidence, generally within 48 hours.
The actual numbers are set locally with land management agencies.

sections.heading: Red Flag Warning
sections.body: A warning-level product denoting high confidence that critical fire weather AND fuel conditions are occurring or will occur, generally within 48 hours. Offices are encouraged to issue with longer lead time when confidence is very high or the fire danger is critical.

sections.heading: Fire Weather Watch
sections.body: Indicates potential for dangerous fire weather, issued 18 to 96 hours ahead of the expected onset. The intent is to alert land managers and the public at least a day in advance.

sections.heading: What red flag criteria combine

items.title: Low humidity
items.detail: Very dry air, below a locally set threshold

items.title: Wind
items.detail: Sustained winds above a locally set threshold, often measured as 20-foot winds

items.title: Dry fuels
items.detail: Fuel dryness or a fire danger rating

sections.banner: All together, commonly for three or more consecutive hours.
sections.note: The national directive sets no numbers at all. Every threshold is a local agreement between the forecast office and land management agencies.

sections.heading: PDS Red Flag Warnings
sections.body: PDS wording is not limited to convective products. Offices have applied it to Red Flag Warnings in rare, extreme fire weather situations, such as the windstorms ahead of the January 2025 Los Angeles fires.

fire-weather.local: Red Flag Warning numeric criteria are NOT national. They are defined locally in coordination with land management agencies and vary considerably by region and fuel type. Do not memorize a humidity or wind number from another office.

quickChecks.q: How far out is a Fire Weather Watch issued?
quickChecks.a: 18 to 96 hours ahead of expected onset. The Red Flag Warning is high confidence, generally within 48 hours.

quickChecks.q: What three things combine for a red flag day?
quickChecks.a: Low humidity, wind, and dry fuels, all together. Weather alone is not enough.

quickChecks.q: Is there a national red flag humidity number?
quickChecks.a: No. Criteria are set locally with land management agencies. Do not memorize another office's number.

tropical-marine.tagline: Lead time is the criterion. Hours matter as much as miles per hour.
tropical-marine.intro: Timing windows define these products. Unlike most of the suite, the number that matters is usually hours of lead time rather than a wind speed.
essentials: Warnings are 36 hours out. Watches are 48 hours out.
Hurricane is 74 mph sustained. Tropical Storm is 39 to 73 mph.
Marine thresholds are lower than land: 34 knots, or 3/4 inch hail.
Storm surge is a separate product from wind and can cover a different area.

sections.heading: How far ahead the products come
sections.intro: The clocks run to the anticipated arrival of tropical-storm-force winds, so preparations can finish before conditions shut them down.
sections.note: Gust criteria are not used for tropical wind products, only sustained winds. Storm surge products are separate from wind products and can cover different areas.

sections.heading: The wind numbers
points: Hurricane products: sustained winds of 74 mph or greater.
Tropical Storm products: sustained winds of 39 to 73 mph.
Storm surge products: life-threatening inundation danger, drawn independently of the wind areas.

sections.heading: Extreme Wind Warning
sections.body: A short-fused warning for the onset of extreme sustained surface winds, 115 mph or greater, in the eyewall of a major hurricane, Category 3 or higher, usually beginning within an hour. It tells people to shelter immediately in an interior room. It is not used for non-tropical wind events.

sections.heading: The marine wind ladder
sections.caption: Sustained winds or frequent gusts, in knots, not associated with a tropical cyclone

sections.heading: Special Marine Warning
sections.body: Issued for winds of 34 knots or greater, hail 3/4 inch or larger, or waterspouts. Short-fused, generally valid up to about two hours.
sections.note: Marine thresholds are LOWER than the land severe criteria, because small vessels are vulnerable at lower wind speeds. Marine hail stayed at 3/4 inch when the land threshold moved to 1.00 inch in 2010.

changes.what: The Small Craft Advisory is slated to become a Small Craft Warning, the notable exception to the plain-language transition, because of the direct threat to life and property.
The NHC forecast cone graphic now also depicts inland tropical storm and hurricane watches and warnings for the U.S., not just the coastline.

quickChecks.q: How far ahead is a Hurricane Warning issued? A Hurricane Watch?
quickChecks.a: Warning 36 hours, Watch 48 hours, measured to the expected arrival of tropical-storm-force winds.

quickChecks.q: What is the Tropical Storm wind range?
quickChecks.a: 39 to 73 mph sustained. Hurricane is 74 mph and up. Gusts are not used.

quickChecks.q: What does an Extreme Wind Warning mean?
quickChecks.a: Eyewall winds of a major hurricane, 115 mph or greater, arriving within about an hour. Shelter immediately in an interior room.

quickChecks.q: Why are marine severe thresholds lower than land?
quickChecks.a: Small vessels are vulnerable at lower speeds. 34 knots, 3/4 inch hail, or a waterspout triggers a Special Marine Warning.

statements.tagline: The everyday products, including the one your reports feed.
statements.intro: The non-warning products that carry most of the day-to-day information flow, including the one your own reports feed.
essentials: A Severe Weather Statement updates or cancels a warning already running.
A Special Weather Statement covers storms just under severe.
Local Storm Reports are where your spotter reports land.
Report as it happens. Late reports mostly have archival value.

sections.heading: Severe Weather Statement (SVS)
sections.body: Follows an active severe thunderstorm or tornado warning: updating its status, shrinking the polygon as the threat passes, or cancelling it. Damage threat tags can be upgraded through an SVS.

sections.heading: Special Weather Statement
sections.body: Covers hazards warranting heightened awareness that fall short of watch, warning or advisory level: roughly 40 to 57 mph gusts, hail under 1 inch, frequent lightning, or funnel clouds not expected to become a tornado threat.

sections.heading: Local Storm Report (LSR)
sections.body: A record of observed severe or significant weather: hail size, wind damage, tornadoes, flooding. Many originate from spotter and public reports.
sections.note: This is the product your reports feed. Report significant observations as they occur, safely. Timely reports have operational value, late reports mostly have archival value.

sections.heading: Hazardous Weather Outlook (HWO)
sections.body: Describes expected hazards over a seven-day period, updated as needed. It includes a spotter activation statement, which is the section telling you whether activation is anticipated.
sections.note: Some offices have retired the text HWO in favor of a graphical version, moving the spotter activation statement into the Area Forecast Discussion. Which form you get depends on your office.

sections.heading: Area Forecast Discussion (AFD)
sections.body: A semi-technical explanation of forecaster reasoning, uncertainty and model disagreement. It is the single most useful product for anticipating how a forecaster is leaning.

changes.what: The Special Weather Statement is scheduled to be discontinued as a headline term, with the information continuing in a bulleted plain-language format and gaining VTEC coding with an .S significance code. The content survives, the headline term goes away.

quickChecks.q: A tornado warning polygon just shrank. What product did that?
quickChecks.a: A Severe Weather Statement, which updates, reduces, or cancels an active warning.

quickChecks.q: Where do your spotter reports end up?
quickChecks.a: In the Local Storm Report. Report as it happens, safely. Late reports mostly have archival value.

quickChecks.q: Which product tells you whether spotter activation is expected?
quickChecks.a: The Hazardous Weather Outlook. Some offices have retired the text version and moved the spotter statement into the AFD.

quickChecks.q: Which product explains what the forecaster is actually thinking?
quickChecks.a: The Area Forecast Discussion, including uncertainty and where the models disagree.

local-maf.tagline: The numbers your office actually uses. Nobody else's.
local-maf.intro: The national modules flag every threshold that is set locally. This module is those numbers for NWS Midland/Odessa: pulled from the fire operating plans that govern MAF, the official NWS snow-criteria dataset, and MAF's own issued products. Nothing here is borrowed from a neighboring office, and where MAF publishes no number, this module says so instead of inventing one.
essentials: Red flag here: humidity 15 percent or less, 20-foot winds 20 mph sustained or 35 gusting, fuels at NFDRS High or drier, all together for 3 or more hours.
Winter Storm Warning snow: 3 inches per event in the basin, 4 inches in the Guadalupes, Davis Mountains and northern tier. The old 12- and 24-hour numbers are gone.
Wind Advisory at 30. High Wind Warning at 40 sustained or 58 gusts, Guadalupes included.
Heat here is air temperature stepped by elevation, not heat index.

sections.heading: Red Flag Warning: the MAF recipe

items.title: RH 15% or less
items.detail: Very dry air, judged on the minimum of a forecast range

items.title: Wind 20 / 35
items.detail: 20-foot winds sustained 20+ mph, or gusts 35+ mph, judged on the midpoint of a range

items.title: Fuels High+
items.detail: NFDRS fire danger rating of High or greater

sections.banner: All three at once, for 3 or more hours.
points: Red Flag Warnings cover events highly likely or imminent, usually 12 to 48 hours out. Fire Weather Watches flag the same threat 18 to 96 hours out.
Conditions just beneath criteria get a Fire Danger Statement rather than a warning.
The Red Flag Threat Index, which rates how far beyond criteria an event goes, was invented at this office.

sections.heading: Winter Storm Warning snow, per event

a.title: Basin and lowlands
rows: Midland, Odessa and the Permian Basin lowlands, 23 zones

b.title: Mountains and northern tier
rows: Guadalupe and Davis mountains, the northern tier and southeast New Mexico, 14 zones

sections.note: Criteria are guidance, not strict thresholds. Forecasters can and do warn below them when timing or impact justifies it, like snow arriving at rush hour.

myths.myth: A Winter Storm Warning here still takes 4 inches in 12 hours or 6 in 24.
myths.truth: Those criteria were retired beginning with the 2023-24 winter season. It is an event total now: 3 inches in the basin, 4 in the Guadalupes, Davis Mountains and northern tier.

myths.myth: The Guadalupe Mountains have their own higher wind thresholds.
myths.truth: Same numbers as the rest of the forecast area: 40 mph sustained or 58 mph gusts. The mountains just meet them far more often.

sections.heading: Wind and fog

rows: Sustained 40 mph, or gusts to 58 mph

sections.note: These match the national defaults, confirmed in MAF's own issued product text rather than assumed.

sections.heading: Dust: the signature hazard
sections.body: MAF is one of the most active dust offices in the country: 45 Dust Storm Warnings in 2025 alone, plus the full advisory suite. The criteria are the national ones from the dust module, and here you will actually use them.
points: Dust Storm Warning and Blowing Dust Warning: visibility 1/4 mile or less.
Dust Advisory and Blowing Dust Advisory: visibility between 1/4 mile and 1 mile.
The convective ones (outflow dust walls off storms) are the polygon products. The synoptic ones (all-day west wind events) are zone-based.

sections.heading: Heat: by elevation, not humidity
sections.body: West Texas heat is dry heat, so MAF writes its heat products in air temperature, not heat index, and the trigger steps down as the terrain climbs. As consistently reflected in MAF's advisories and forecast discussions: around 95 in the mountains, around 100 in the higher elevations, around 105 in the basin and plains, and around 110 along the Rio Grande, where Extreme Heat Warning territory runs roughly 110 to 115.
sections.note: MAF has never formally published heat criteria. These tiers come from an audit of three and a half years of their issued products, so treat them as strong guidance rather than gospel, and expect the far-northeastern zones, the more humid corner, to occasionally use heat index instead.

sections.heading: Cold
sections.body: Since the October 2024 rebuild, MAF issues Cold Weather Advisories for wind chills roughly in the plus-15-to-below-zero range depending on zone, with the warm Presidio Valley held to a colder bar, and Extreme Cold Warnings when wind chills run around 5 below zero and colder. Freeze products use the standard 32 degrees at the growing season bookends, typically October through December and April.
sections.note: Also from the product archive: MAF essentially never issues a Frost Advisory. Zero were issued from April 2023 through August 2026. Around here, cold that matters is freeze or wind chill.

sections.heading: What is deliberately missing here
sections.body: MAF publishes no Winter Weather Advisory snowfall number, no formal heat or cold criteria, and no office criteria page at all. Where that is the case, this module says so rather than borrowing a neighboring office's numbers. When in doubt during an event, the WHAT line of the product itself tells you what the forecaster is treating as criteria.

local-maf.local: This whole module is the local numbers the other nine keep telling you to look up. Sources: the Texas and Southwest Area fire weather operating plans, the official NWS heavy-snow criteria dataset at weather.gov/snow-criteria, and MAF's own issued products and discussions. If a neighboring office's webpage disagrees with these, it does not apply here.

changes.what: Winter Storm Warning snow criteria moved from 12- and 24-hour totals to per-event totals nationwide; MAF's are 3 inches (basin) and 4 inches (high mountains, northern tier and southeast New Mexico).
changes.when: Beginning with the 2023-24 winter season; the current directive carries it forward.

quickChecks.q: Recite the red flag recipe for this office.
quickChecks.a: Humidity 15 percent or less, 20-foot winds 20+ mph sustained or 35+ gusting, NFDRS High or greater, all together for 3 or more hours.

quickChecks.q: Snow is coming to Midland proper. How much triggers a Winter Storm Warning?
quickChecks.a: About 3 inches for the event. In the Guadalupes, Davis mountains or the northern tier, 4 inches.

quickChecks.q: What wind speed triggers a plain Wind Advisory here?
quickChecks.a: Sustained winds around 30 mph. At 40 sustained or 58 gusting it becomes a High Wind Warning.

quickChecks.q: Does MAF use heat index?
quickChecks.a: Almost never. Heat products here run on air temperature, stepped by elevation: roughly 105 does it in the basin and plains.

quickChecks.q: How many Dust Storm Warnings did this office issue in 2025?
quickChecks.a: 45. Dust is the signature local hazard. Warning means 1/4 mile visibility or less.

storm-structure.tagline: What you are looking at, and whether to report it.
storm-structure.intro: The other modules teach the products. This one teaches the sky: how storms are built, which cloud features matter, and how to tell a tornado from the six things that impersonate one. Sourced from the NWS spotter field guides, the NWS glossary, NSSL and the WMO cloud atlas.
essentials: Wall cloud: isolated, under the rain-free base, air rising in. Shelf cloud: leading edge, air pushing out. Inflow versus outflow is the whole game.
A debris cloud under a funnel means tornado. Do not wait for the condensation funnel to reach the ground.
Watch a suspicious feature for organized rotation on a vertical axis before you report it.
Mammatus and shelf clouds look terrifying. Neither one is a tornado signal.

sections.heading: The life of a thunderstorm
sections.body: Every thunderstorm runs the same arc. Developing: an updraft builds a towering cumulus, little to no rain. Mature: precipitation drags down a downdraft that coexists with the updraft, and this is when hail, damaging wind and tornadoes are most likely. Dissipating: the storm's own gust front pushes out and cuts off the warm inflow, the downdraft takes over, and the rain fades.
points: An ordinary single cell lives roughly 30 to 60 minutes. Storms that keep building new updrafts can go for hours.
The anvil forms where the updraft stops rising and spreads out. A sharp-edged, solid anvil means a strong updraft; thin and wispy means a weak one.

items.alt: Two crisp towering cumulus clouds with hard cauliflower tops
items.caption: Towering cumulus: hard cauliflower top, no anvil yet. The developing stage.
items.credit: Ralph F. Kresge, NOAA Photo Library (wea00088)

items.alt: Large cumulonimbus with a flattened spreading anvil top
items.caption: The flattened, spreading anvil makes it a cumulonimbus. This is the thunderstorm cloud.

sections.heading: The four storm modes

rows: Brief hail, downburst winds, rarely a weak tornado
New cells keep forming on the gust front; the cluster outlives its cells by hours
Downbursts, moderate hail, flooding, occasional weak tornadoes
A line of storms, sometimes hundreds of miles long
Damaging straight-line winds above all; quick spin-up tornadoes
One persistent rotating updraft, lasting hours
The majority of intense tornadoes, giant hail, extreme wind

sections.note: QLCS tornadoes spin up fast along the line, often near a break in the line or on the north end of a bowing segment, and offer far less visual warning than supercell tornadoes. On radar, damaging wind concentrates at the apex of a bow echo.

sections.heading: Supercell anatomy
sections.body: Learn this one picture and the sky starts making sense. The updraft is the storm's engine; the rain-free base beneath it is where the important features live. Precipitation falls ahead (the forward flank), and a second, drier downdraft wraps around the back of the rotation: the rear flank downdraft, or RFD.
points: The wall cloud, if one forms, hangs under the rain-free base and marks the strongest updraft. Tornadoes are most likely near the intersection of the updraft and the RFD.
An overshooting top that persists means a very strong updraft. If it suddenly collapses, a burst of hail or damaging wind may be imminent.
A clear slot eating into the clouds behind the wall cloud is the RFD made visible, and it often precedes or accompanies tornado formation.
Mesocyclone is a radar term for the storm-scale rotation. On radar, precipitation wrapping around it draws the classic hook echo.
The flanking line of stair-stepped towers feeding the storm signals organization, and gust-front tornadoes can occasionally form along it.

items.alt: Classic supercell at dusk with wide anvil and striated updraft tower
items.caption: A classic supercell near Humboldt, Nebraska: anvil spread wide, striated tower marking the rotating updraft.
items.credit: Stephen Corfidi, NOAA/NWS SPC; NOAA Photo Library (wea03319)

sections.heading: The three supercell flavors
sections.body: Classic supercells look like the diagram. Low-precipitation (LP) supercells, common near the dryline, look skeletal and translucent, but can still drop very large hail you cannot see falling. High-precipitation (HP) supercells bury their structure in rain, and they may be the most common type nationwide.
sections.note: HP supercells are the dangerous ones for spotters: the tornado can be completely rain-wrapped. The field guide's rule is absolute: do not drive through precipitation to see if a tornado is present.

sections.heading: Wall cloud versus shelf cloud
sections.body: The single most important distinction in spotting, because they are reported for opposite reasons and confused constantly.

sections.heading: The tells, side by side

a.title: Wall cloud
rows: Isolated lowering under the rain-free base, trailing side
Inflow: rising, may rotate on a vertical axis
Holds position, slopes upward away from it
Updraft core; tornado potential when rotating

b.title: Shelf cloud
rows: Long wedge on the leading edge, along the gust front
Outflow: pushing out and down, ragged underside
Moves away from it, slopes downward
Damaging straight-line wind; usually not tornadic

sections.note: A shelf cloud can appear to roll on a horizontal axis. A wall cloud rotates on a vertical axis. If it spins like a merry-go-round, pay attention; if it rolls like a rolling pin, it is outflow.

items.alt: Wall cloud with tail cloud hanging beneath a rain-free storm base
items.caption: The real thing: wall cloud with tail cloud under a rain-free base, Oklahoma-Texas border, 1980. Isolated, attached, right next to the rain.

items.alt: Wedge-shaped shelf cloud leading a thunderstorm gust front
items.caption: Shelf cloud on a gust front, New Mexico, 1982. A long wedge on the storm's leading edge: outflow, wind.

sections.heading: When a wall cloud gets serious

items.title: Persistence
items.detail: It lasts 10 minutes or more, holding position relative to the rain

items.title: Rotation
items.detail: Persistent, organized rotation on a vertical axis

items.title: Violent motion
items.detail: Cloud elements rising rapidly into it, strong surface inflow

sections.banner: Rotating wall cloud = urgent report. Rotation can precede the tornado by up to an hour.
sections.note: Fewer than half of observed wall clouds ever produce a tornado, and a non-rotating wall cloud is essentially harmless. That is exactly why your report of WHICH kind you see has operational value.

myths.myth: The funnel has to reach the ground before it counts as a tornado.
myths.truth: A rotating dust or debris cloud beneath the funnel confirms a tornado, full stop. In dry country with high cloud bases, the condensation funnel may never visibly reach the ground at all.

myths.myth: That ragged dangling cloud is a developing funnel.
myths.truth: Probably scud: detached, wind-torn fragments that mimic funnels but do not rotate and are not attached. Wall clouds are always attached; funnels always rotate.

myths.myth: A spinning dust cloud under the gust front is a tornado.
myths.truth: That is a gustnado, an outflow eddy with no connection to cloud-base rotation. Officially not a tornado, but still report it: it is a wind hazard.

myths.myth: No supercell, no mesocyclone, so no tornado is possible.
myths.truth: Landspouts are true tornadoes that form without a mesocyclone, often under a still-growing tower, with no wall cloud and little radar warning.

items.alt: Tornado whose condensation funnel stops well above the ground while a dust cloud swirls at the surface
items.caption: The most important photo in this module. The funnel is nowhere near the ground, but the dust cloud at the surface means this IS a tornado. Cordell, Oklahoma, 1981.

items.alt: White condensation funnel hanging in the air, not reaching the ground
items.caption: A funnel cloud near El Reno, Oklahoma: rotating, aloft, no debris beneath. Not yet a tornado.

items.alt: Ragged low scud cloud fragments beneath a developing storm
items.caption: Ragged scud fragments under a storm. Detached and not rotating: not a funnel, not a wall cloud.

items.alt: Dust whirl spinning along a gust front in an urban area
items.caption: A gustnado along a gust front, Louisville, 2005. Ground debris with no cloud-base rotation above it: not a tornado, still a hazard.

sections.heading: The five questions before you report
sections.body: The Spotter's Field Guide gives a screening test for any suspicious feature. If the answer to any question is no, it is probably not a tornado.
points: Can I see it clearly?
Is the feature attached to the thunderstorm base?
Is it near the updraft, where tornadoes actually develop?
Is there organized rotation within the feature?
If it appears to be a tornado, is there debris?
sections.note: Report only what you see, not what you think you see. Give the event's location, not your own. If you are unsure, report anyway and say you are unsure.

sections.heading: Reading the sky: the cloud families
points: Decode any name from four roots: cirro = curl of hair, cumulo = heap, strato = layer, nimbo = rain.
The trap: alto means high in Latin, but the alto clouds are the MIDDLE family.
Cumulus and cumulonimbus keep their bases low but can tower through every level; many courses teach them as their own vertical development family.
Altocumulus castellanus, turrets sprouting from mid-level cloud, is an official sign of instability aloft and can precede rapid thunderstorm development.
Towering cumulus becomes a cumulonimbus the moment the top glaciates and flattens into an anvil.

items.alt: Field of smooth pouch-like mammatus clouds
items.caption: Mammatus over Hobart, Oklahoma, 1977. They often accompany severe storms but do not produce severe weather. A photo opportunity, not a tornado signal.

sections.heading: Spotting at night
sections.body: Use lightning flashes to illuminate storm structure, and watch the horizon for the blue-green flashes of power lines arcing, which indicate damaging winds at that spot. A loud roar may mean a tornado is close, but not every tornado roars and some straight-line winds do.
sections.note: The field guide is blunt: nighttime storm spotting from a vehicle is dangerous and not recommended. Fixed position, escape route known, and more caution than daylight.

quickChecks.q: A ragged lowering hangs near the storm base. What two things decide whether it is worth reporting?
quickChecks.a: Is it attached, and does it have organized rotation on a vertical axis? Scud is detached and does not rotate. Watch it for a minute or two before deciding.

quickChecks.q: The funnel is only halfway down, but dust is whirling beneath it. Tornado or funnel cloud?
quickChecks.a: Tornado. A debris cloud under the funnel confirms the circulation is on the ground. Report it as a tornado.

quickChecks.q: A long wedge of cloud is racing at you ahead of the rain. What is it and what does it mean?
quickChecks.a: A shelf cloud on the gust front. It means damaging straight-line wind, not usually a tornado. Brace and report the wind.

quickChecks.q: What makes a supercell a supercell?
quickChecks.a: A persistent rotating updraft, the mesocyclone. It can last hours and produces the majority of intense tornadoes.

quickChecks.q: Which lifecycle stage brings the severe weather?
quickChecks.a: Mature: updraft and downdraft coexisting. Developing is updraft only, dissipating is downdraft only.

radar-basics.tagline: What the radar sees, what it misses, and why you still matter.
radar-basics.intro: Radar is the most powerful severe weather tool ever built, and it still cannot see a tornado. This module covers what the beam actually measures, the ways it lies to you at distance, the signatures worth knowing, and where your eyes fit into a system that depends on them.
essentials: Radar measures returned power, not rain. Everything else is inferred.
The beam climbs as the earth curves away: at 100 miles you are looking 12,000 feet up, and the low levels are simply not sampled.
Velocity is motion toward or away from THE RADAR, never a compass direction.
Radar usually cannot resolve the tornado itself, and cannot see below cloud base except close in. It shows rotation; you supply the ground truth.

sections.heading: What the radar is actually doing
sections.body: About 160 WSR-88D radars cover the country, run jointly by the National Weather Service, the FAA and the military. Each one transmits a brief pulse of energy, then listens for the echo. Timing the round trip gives range; the strength of the echo gives reflectivity. That is the whole trick.
points: The pulses are astonishingly brief. Across a full hour, the radar spends only about seven seconds transmitting and the rest listening.
Reflectivity is reported in dBZ, a compressed logarithmic scale running from about -35 to +85, because raw returned power spans an absurd range of values.
The WSR-88D uses a 10 cm wavelength, which passes through heavy precipitation far better than the shorter wavelengths used by most other radars.

items.alt: NEXRAD radar dome with a large supercell thunderstorm behind it
items.caption: A WSR-88D radome in South Dakota with a hail-producing supercell behind it. The dome protects the dish; the dish is what scans.
items.credit: Eric Kurth, NOAA/NWS; NOAA Photo Library (Wea01195)

sections.heading: The two operating modes

rows: Scans slower, sweeps fewer angles, and two of its patterns use a longer pulse for extra sensitivity. Full sweep takes roughly 7 to 10 minutes.
Quiet weather. The extra sensitivity is why you see birds, bugs, dust and smoke.
Scans faster through more angles, roughly 4 to 6 minutes for a full volume.
Anything convective. The radar switches itself over once returns cross a threshold.

sections.note: Modern radars also cheat in your favor: they can cut a volume short when nothing is happening aloft, and insert extra sweeps of the lowest tilt. With those enabled, the lowest slice, where tornadoes live, can refresh roughly every 90 seconds instead of every four minutes.

sections.heading: Reading dBZ

rows: Extremely heavy precipitation, likely including water-coated hail

sections.note: Guidelines, not measurements. Returned power scales with drop diameter to the SIXTH power, so a handful of big drops returns as much as a downpour of small ones. Tropical rain routinely shows only 35 to 45 dBZ while dropping a foot of water.

sections.heading: The single most important limitation
sections.body: The beam leaves the radar in a nearly straight line. The earth curves away beneath it. The result is that the farther a storm sits from the radar, the higher up you are looking at it, until the part of the storm that matters most is entirely below the beam.
points: At about 100 miles, the lowest scan is roughly 12,000 feet above ground.
The beam also widens as it travels, spreading about 1,000 feet every 10 miles, so it is nearly two miles across at 100 miles out. Small features blur into nothing.
Directly above the radar is the cone of silence: volume scans top out at 19.5 degrees of elevation, so storms overhead go unsampled above that angle.
Features are not stacked vertically either. Beyond about 50 miles, a low-level circulation can sit several miles away from the mid-level rotation shown on your screen.

items.alt: NOAA chart showing the lowest radar scan rising and widening with range
items.caption: The lowest scan, plotted against range. The beam climbs and fattens the whole way out.

items.alt: Radar reflectivity showing a sharply defined hook echo from a nearby radar
items.caption: Jarrell, Texas from 20 miles away: beam height about 1,300 feet. The hook is unmistakable and an EF-3 is on the ground.

items.alt: Radar reflectivity of the same storm from a distant radar, with the hook barely visible
items.caption: The same storm, same moment, from 98 miles: beam height about 11,600 feet. The hook is faint at best.

myths.myth: That distant storm looks like it is falling apart on radar.
myths.truth: It may be doing nothing of the kind. As a storm moves away, the beam samples higher and higher in it, where rotation is weaker. Official guidance is to assume circulations are at least as strong below the beam as they look on the lowest slice, and never to call a storm weakening just because it moved away.

sections.heading: Base versus composite reflectivity

a.title: Base reflectivity
rows: Shows hook echoes and outflow boundaries
The strongest part of a storm may sit above the slice

b.title: Composite reflectivity
rows: The maximum return from every elevation, merged
Only after a full volume scan
Fast read on which storms are strongest

sections.note: Use composite to find the storms that matter, then base to look at the one you care about.

sections.heading: Velocity: motion toward you, not motion north
sections.body: Doppler velocity measures only the part of a target motion that is aimed directly at or away from the radar. Motion straight across the beam reads as zero no matter how fast it is, and the displayed speed is always less than or equal to the true speed.
points: Green is inbound, toward the radar. Red is outbound, away from it. Brighter means faster.
Inbound beside outbound at the same range means rotation. The tighter the pair, the stronger the rotation.
If the two maxima are strung out along the same radial instead, that is convergence or divergence, not rotation.
Base velocity includes the storm motion itself, which can mask rotation in a fast-moving storm. Storm-relative velocity subtracts that motion out.

items.alt: Side by side radar reflectivity and velocity showing a hook echo and a tight rotation couplet
items.caption: Reflectivity and velocity of the same storm: hook on the left, tight inbound-outbound couplet on the right, tornado in progress near Oklahoma City.

sections.heading: Rotation has a size hierarchy
points: A mesocyclone is a storm-scale rotation, typically 2 to 6 miles across. It is a radar term for a signature meeting criteria for strength, depth and duration, and it is far bigger than any tornado inside it. You cannot see a mesocyclone; you see the wall cloud beneath it.

A tornadic vortex signature is much smaller and tighter, essentially adjacent radar gates of opposite motion. It strongly raises the odds of a tornado without guaranteeing one, and often appears aloft before touchdown.
Neither one is a tornado. Both are rotation the radar can resolve, which is a different thing.

items.alt: Radar reflectivity showing a classic hook echo on a supercell
items.caption: A hook echo: precipitation wrapped around the mesocyclone by the rear flank downdraft, in the right-rear of the storm. Favorable, not proof.

items.alt: Radar reflectivity showing a bowing line segment with annotation arrows
items.caption: A bow echo. The damaging straight-line winds run at the apex; the north end can spin up tornadoes.

items.alt: Radar reflectivity showing a spike extending away from a storm core
items.caption: A hail spike: energy bouncing between huge hailstones and the ground arrives late, so the radar paints a false spike pointing away from itself. A strong hint of severe hail.

sections.heading: What dual-polarization added
sections.body: Between 2011 and 2013 the network gained the ability to pulse vertically as well as horizontally, which means the radar can now infer the SHAPE of what it is hitting, not just how much is there.
points: Differential reflectivity compares the two. Flattened raindrops read above zero. Tumbling hail looks round to the radar and reads near zero, so high reflectivity with near-zero differential reflectivity says hail.

Correlation coefficient measures how alike the targets in the beam are. Above 0.97 is uniform rain or snow. Between 0.80 and 0.97 suggests a mix, or hail. Below 0.80 means the beam is full of things that are nothing like each other: birds, insects, smoke, or debris.
Specific differential phase tracks how much the beam is slowed by what it passes through, which sharpens heavy-rainfall and flash-flood estimates.

items.alt: Four-panel radar display showing reflectivity, two velocity tilts, and correlation coefficient with a debris signature
items.caption: A tornado debris signature. Hook in reflectivity, tight couplet in velocity at two tilts, and a circled collapse in correlation coefficient exactly where the couplet is. That is lofted debris: a tornado on the ground doing damage.

items.alt: Radar panels showing a strong velocity couplet with no drop in correlation coefficient
items.caption: And the counter-example that matters: a large tornado was in progress here, with no correlation coefficient drop at all. No debris signature never means no tornado.

sections.note: A debris signature confirms; it does not predict. By the time debris is aloft, damage is already happening. And the drop must be co-located with the couplet, or it is not a debris signature at all.

rows: A blotch of returns permanently around the radar
Buildings, hills and terrain reflecting the beam. It does not move or evolve.
Convincing but fake precipitation, often at night
A temperature inversion bends the beam into the ground. Check a neighboring radar for a second opinion.
Storms mysteriously weaker in one direction
Terrain, buildings or wind farms blocking the beam. Anything downrange looks weaker than it is.
Purple haze where data should be
The radar cannot tell which pulse an echo belongs to, so it discards the data.
A ring of enhanced returns around the radar
Melting snowflakes coated in water look like huge raindrops. Easiest to spot on higher tilts.
Weak returns directly behind an intense core
Energy absorbed on the way through. Less severe on these radars than most, but real.

sections.heading: Where you come in
sections.body: Radar usually cannot resolve the tornado itself. That is not a limitation of your app or of any particular radar; it is physics. Within a few tens of miles the beam is already wider than a tornado, it cannot see below cloud base except very close in, and what it detects is rotation. Most detected circulations never produce a tornado at all.
points: Radar tells you which storm to watch and where on it to look. That is enormous, and it is not the same as knowing what is happening.
Your report of what is actually occurring under the storm is what closes the loop, and it matters most exactly where radar is weakest: far from the site, in terrain, and below the beam.
Use both. Check the structure on radar, then confirm with your eyes, and report what you see.
sections.note: This is why an unwarned tornado is usually a coverage story. In one documented case the nearest beam was 13,000 feet up, showing barely any echo at all, while an EF-1 was on the ground underneath it.

quickChecks.q: Your screen shows 60 dBZ. How much rain is falling?
quickChecks.a: Unknown. dBZ measures returned power, and a few large drops return as much as many small ones. It suggests heavy precipitation and possibly hail, but it is not a rainfall measurement.

quickChecks.q: A storm 100 miles away shows weak rotation. What should you assume?
quickChecks.a: That the beam is about 12,000 feet up and two miles wide, so the real circulation below it is at least as strong as what you see, possibly much stronger.

quickChecks.q: Green sits right beside red on velocity. Rotation or not?
quickChecks.a: Rotation only if the two maxima are side by side at the same range from the radar. Strung out along the same radial, it is convergence or divergence.

quickChecks.q: Does green mean the wind is blowing west?
quickChecks.a: No. Green means motion toward the radar, wherever the radar happens to be. Velocity is radar-relative, never a compass direction.

quickChecks.q: Correlation coefficient collapses right on top of a tight couplet. What does that mean?
quickChecks.a: A tornado debris signature: debris is being lofted, so a tornado is on the ground doing damage. It confirms rather than predicts, and its absence proves nothing.

quickChecks.q: Radar shows a textbook hook. Do you report a tornado?
quickChecks.a: No. You report what you can see. A hook means precipitation wrapping a rotating updraft, which is favorable, but the radar cannot resolve the tornado itself and cannot see below cloud base at that range.
